segments.words: Well, sleeping in and him out here working, and you know, stuff like that. And all he had a heart as big as all outdoors for the family, but not for anybody else. He was straight, he was a straight shooter. By God, he expected the other fellow to be that way, too.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: I can't help but think that the reason he was that way is because he had it so tough when he was a kid.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: He tells about, well, he was only eight years old when he had to go out and herd cattle for this big landowner over in Sweden. And didn't have no shoes, and cold in the fall, frosty, and when a cow would urinate, he'd run up and stick his feet in it to warm his feet.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Pretty rough for an eight-year-old, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, and working for somebody else besides your own family, too.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: That might have been one of the reasons why he was so easy on us, that he didn't want us to have it like he had it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, in my opinion, if you were going to be one or the other, it'd be a lot better to be nice to your family and mean to the outside world than to be nice to the outside world and mean to the family.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: He was mean to others, but he was awful strict with the other fella. He better be on the up-and-up, because that's what he expected. And I remember him telling about herding these darn cows, and then there was one day it was warm and sunshine, he was up on the hillside, he was only eight years old, and laid down there and went to sleep. And of course the darn cows had to go down to get in this fellow's oak field or something. The old fella seen that, and he'd come up there, and to wake my dad, he just kicked him. Just gave him a hell of a kick.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: I know that's set in my dad's memory all the time. He said if he ever went back to Sweden, he was going to kill him. By the time he got big enough that he could do that, well that old fella would probably sit in an old rocking chair somewhere.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the deal on that, that most of the families, like his family, just kind of worked for this guy?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Yes, it was just slaves, I guess. A multitude. He met, they had to ask permission to go and gather up some cute twigs up and brush from wood. I can't imagine that that, I can understand where that would make a man feel that everybody better deal with him as an equal.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: And he left home when he was 13 years old, and he'd never seen his folks after that. But his, but his sister, it's his sister on that picture.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: His sister came out here then, came to, not only to the United States, but right out here and lived in Deary. So he did see his sister after.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Do you suppose he was the oldest, your dad?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: I don't know. Probably. I don't know whether she was.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: I said he, do you suppose he was the oldest?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: I kind of think so. He was probably the oldest, because he had to go to sea and so on.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think that he had a real dislike of aristocrats, or that kind of system, a feudal system?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Indeed, indeed. He never liked to see anyone take advantage of the other fellow.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: But that's, that was memories that stuck in my dad all his life. Remembering that herd and that cow, and I'm getting kicked. So he had a big heart for kids, especially us kids. Spoiled as rotten.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you ever get in any, any fights that you remember yourself?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: No, I remember he wanted to get in a fight when he was about 70 years old. You, you say you. I'm talking about you. But I've been in a fight. He says did you ever. Oh yeah, I've been in one or two. Not in the mountain. I was always sissy.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Your dad raised you a sissy, huh?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Don't strike me as a guy that would turn the other cheek. I left some marks on him.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Now he met your mother when she was cooking in one of these saw camps, one of these sawmill camps, didn't he?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Yeah, she was cooking for a sawmill over here. When my dad met her.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: A local girl?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: No, no, she come out from Iowa to visit her sister that was out here, and liked it out here, and she and my dad was married.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: That was about 19, what, must have been 1903.

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Do you imagine?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say this about dealing fair, that he expected other deal fair with him, I'm just wondering more as an example of what that kind of thing would be.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I mean, are you thinking like business deals or exchanging work and that kind of a thing?

segments.speaker: Oscar Olson or Hazel Olson
segments.words: Yeah, well, your word had to be good.
